extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, inventors and other readers seeking an overview of Canadian novelty and non-obviousness law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the Canadian legal standards for patentability focused on novelty (section 28.2) and non-obviousness/inventive step (section 28.3), including case-law tests and practical doctrines (anticipation, enablement, obvious-to-try, commercial success). Useful as a reference for assessing whether a claimed invention meets Canadian patentability thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty requirement (s.28.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 28.2(1) of the Patent Act: the subject-matter defined by a claim must not have been disclosed (a) more than one year before the filing date by the applicant (or someone who obtained knowledge from the applicant) such that it became publicly available, (b) before the claim date by a person not mentioned in (a) such that it became publicly available, or (c) in an earlier Canadian patent application filed by another person with an earlier filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This codifies that an invention must be 'new' — prior public disclosure anywhere (publications, displays, prior patents/applications) will bar patentability. The statute creates a one-year applicant grace period; earlier secret but unpublished abandoned applications do not constitute disclosure. Private, non-public documents (internal memos) do not count as public disclosure. Ignorance of prior disclosure is no excuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant disclosure / grace period (s.28.2(1)(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 28.2(1)(a) provides a one-year grace period allowing claims to subject-matter in a Canadian patent application up to twelve months after public disclosure by the applicant or someone who obtained knowledge from the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grace period permits inventors to disclose to investors or the public without immediate loss of Canadian patent rights for up to one year. Because the grace period is not universal internationally, reliance on it is limited for foreign filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure by another party (public availability)
rubrics_metrics.description: If subject-matter was disclosed by another person in Canada or elsewhere in such a manner that it became available to the public, a patent cannot be granted on the same subject-matter in Canada.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures that make the invention publicly available include publications, patents, and public displays. The prior disclosure must be sufficiently detailed and self-contained to be anticipatory; mere sale or use without disclosure is generally insufficient unless it amounts to enabling disclosure (see Baker Petrolite principles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation — Reeves Brothers eight-pronged formulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reeves Brothers (Justice Gibson) enumerated eight formulations used to determine whether prior art is anticipatory (e.g., give an exact prior description; give directions which will inevitably result in something within the claims; give clear and unmistakable directions; convey information so a person grappling with the same problem can say 'that gives me what I wish', etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The eight formulations were not intended to be cumulative; they are various ways courts have expressed the test for anticipation. A single prior document can be anticipatory if it meets the relevant formulation(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation by publication — Beloit standard
rubrics_metrics.description: From Beloit Canada Ltd. v. Valmet Oy: a prior single publication must contain all information, which for practical purposes is needed to produce the claimed invention without exercise of any inventive skill; the publication must contain clear directions such that a skilled person following it would in every case and without possibility of error be led to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation requires a single prior disclosure that is enabling and sufficiently specific; aggregation of multiple documents to reach the invention does not establish anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation by prior use or sale — Baker Petrolite principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Baker Petrolite listed principles for anticipation by prior use or sale, including that sale/use alone is insufficient; the sale or use must amount to enabling disclosure; analysis/reverse-engineering can make a sold product an enabling disclosure if the composition can be discovered by known analytical techniques without inventive skill; actual analysis by the public is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: enabling disclosure is required for anticipation by sale/use; reverse engineering that a skilled person could perform with routine techniques can make the invention publicly available; the amount of time/work required is irrelevant except to the extent inventive skill is needed; exact reproduction of the sold product is not necessary — what matters is disclosure of subject-matter within the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apotex two-part test for anticipation: disclosure and enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court in Apotex adopted a two-branch test: (1) prior disclosure — the prior art must indicate to a person skilled in the art that it discloses the special advantages of the later invention; and (2) enablement — the prior art must enable the skilled person to make or perform the later invention without undue burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure and enablement are distinct: disclosure establishes that the prior art points to the invention; enablement assesses whether a skilled person could actually make it without undue burden. Routine trials are acceptable; prolonged or arduous trial-and-error is not. The skilled person's common general knowledge may be used to supplement the prior patent. The prior patent must be considered as a whole (specification and claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement — non-exhaustive factors (from Apotex)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court listed four non-exhaustive factors for enablement: consider the prior patent as a whole incl. specification and claims; allow the skilled person to use common general knowledge; require enough information to perform/make the later invention without undue burden (taking the field's nature into account); and obvious errors/omissions that a skilled person could readily correct do not defeat enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of undue burden depends on the field: where experimentation is common, the threshold for undue burden is higher. If inventive steps would be required to implement the disclosure, the prior art is not enabling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earlier patent application / priority (first-to-file)
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority in Canada is determined by order of applications — an earlier Canadian application will bar a later one; Canada uses a first-to-file approach for priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An earlier application that remains secret because it is abandoned/withdrawn before publication does not constitute disclosure. Filing earlier is crucial to secure priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obviousness requirement (s.28.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 28.3 of the Patent Act: the subject-matter of a claim must not have been obvious on the claim date to a person skilled in the art, having regard to information disclosed more than one year before the filing date by the applicant (or someone who obtained knowledge from the applicant) and information disclosed before the claim date by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This codifies the requirement that an invention include some element of inventiveness beyond the prior art. Like s.28.2, s.28.3 includes a one-year grace period for applicant disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled in the art (hypothetical benchmark)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'man skilled in the art' is a hypothetical technician 'having no scintilla of inventiveness or imagination; a paragon of deduction and dexterity, wholly devoid of intuition' — the benchmark for assessing obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The characteristics attributed to the skilled person (education, experience, common general knowledge) materially affect the obviousness inquiry because they determine what would have been obvious or routine at the relevant time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Windsurfing/Apotex four-step obviousness test
rubrics_metrics.description: The four-step approach (adopted in Apotex from Windsurfing/Windsurfing-type tests): (1) identify the notional person skilled in the art and their common general knowledge; (2) identify the inventive concept of the claim (or construe the claim if the inventive concept is not readily apparent); (3) identify the differences between the state of the art and the inventive concept/claim; (4) without knowledge of the alleged invention, ask whether those differences would have been obvious to the skilled person or required any degree of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each step is crucial and factual/legal disputes often turn on characterizing the skilled person, construing the claim, or identifying relevant prior art. The 'viewed without any knowledge of the alleged invention' caveat is central to avoiding hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try doctrine and its non-exhaustive factors
rubrics_metrics.description: In fields involving routine experimentation (e.g., pharmaceuticals), an invention may be obvious if it would have been 'obvious to try' — the Court provided non-exclusive factors: whether it is self-evident that what is being tried ought to work and there are a finite number of identified predictable solutions; the extent, nature and amount of effort required (routine trials vs prolonged/arduous experimentation); and whether prior art provided a motive to find the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the required experimentation is extensive or unpredictable, a court may find it was not obvious to try and thus allow patentability. Where predictable solutions are finite and routine, 'obvious to try' can render a claim obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success and secondary indicia of non-obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success of a patented product is a factor that may support a finding of non-obviousness, but taken alone it is not conclusive; courts consider it alongside other factors such as novelty, superiority, widespread use, preference over alternatives, and expert reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success can corroborate inventiveness especially when combined with other evidence (e.g., device is novel and superior, used widely and in preference to alternatives, competitors had not thought of the combination, amazement on first publication). It is one of many contextual factors courts may weigh.
